desc:
A grid has 1 in cells where a person lives and 0 in empty cells. All people want to meet in a single cell of the grid (any cell, occupied or not). Everyone walks to the meeting cell, and the distance for one person is the Manhattan distance |r1 - r2| + |c1 - c2|.

Return the smallest possible sum of all walking distances.

For example, [[1,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]] gives 4: both people can meet at the centre cell (or on any shortest path between them).
constraints: The grid contains at least two people (two cells equal to 1)
hints: The Manhattan distance splits into a row part and a column part, and the meeting cell can pick its row and column independently.
For one dimension this is the 'closest point to many points' problem: the sum of absolute distances is minimized at a median.
Collect the row index of every person (already sorted if you scan row by row), and the column indices (sort them, or scan column by column). Add the distances to the two medians.
editorial: The total distance is sum |r_p - R| + sum |c_p - C| for meeting cell (R, C). The two sums depend on different unknowns, so we minimize each separately. Each is a sum of absolute deviations from one point, which is minimized at the median of the coordinates.

Scanning the grid in row-major order produces the row coordinates already sorted; scanning in column-major order does the same for columns (or just sort). Take rows[m // 2] and cols[m // 2], where m is the number of people, and sum the distances. The cost is O(rows * cols) time. Note that even if the median cell is not occupied, it is still a legal meeting cell and lies inside the grid.
